intro: San Francisco spent the week finding rules that point at the wrong thing. A SoMa childcare center absorbed 13 state inspections and then closed because the money ran out, a two-year-old ban on rent-setting algorithms has produced zero lawsuits while asking rents rose 14 percent in four months, and the data center moratorium both congressional candidates are arguing over would not touch a single server hall already running here. Four editions, 18 items, and most of them turn on the same gap between the rule as written and the place the decision actually gets made.
ai_disclosure: This digest is composed with AI assistance from the week's published Brief items, then reviewed and edited by Eric before publish. AI does not write the news. Original reporting is always linked, always credited.

top_stories.source_headline: SF sheriff accused of hiding TV crew's role in child exploitation sting
top_stories.one_line: Defense lawyers said the San Francisco Sheriff's Office left Chris Hansen's television production crew out of arrest reports in a July child exploitation sting that produced five arrests.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The sheriff's body camera policy exempts interviews run by a television production, so the most legally consequential 20 minutes of the operation were the only part with no recording. That was not a loophole someone found later, it was the policy as written, and the district attorney wanted a confidentiality agreement signed before the defense could read the sheriff's contract with the production company.

top_stories.source_headline: SF tried to ban its way to lower rents. Then the AI boom hit
top_stories.one_line: Two years after San Francisco banned landlords from using rent-setting algorithms, the law has produced no civil actions and apartment asking rents rose 14 percent between March and July.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The city banned the mechanism it blamed for high rents and then watched rents set records, which turned the law into a test of whether anyone had named the mechanism correctly. A UC Davis economist read the spike as a demand shock from high-paying AI jobs entering a market already short on supply after years of underbuilding, not collusion. Aaron Peskin, who wrote the ban, argued it worked by naming and shaming before a trillion dollars of capital arrived.

top_stories.source_headline: Their roommate died. Then their rent more than tripled to $9,250
top_stories.one_line: After his roommate of 26 years died, Dustin Lee was told to pay $9,250 or leave the Church Street flat where three subtenants had been splitting $2,979.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The protections San Francisco calls the strongest in the nation stop at the master tenant, and nobody counts how many people live in the layer underneath. The owner was SF Owner LLC, a Delaware entity formed six weeks before it took the building in a 2024 foreclosure, sharing an address with Ballast Investments, which with Brookfield became the largest apartment landlord in San Francisco by buying Veritas's defaulted debt at a discount.

top_stories.source_headline: SF's Data Center Debate Heats Up As One Site Looms Large on the County Line
top_stories.one_line: The Frisc found at least six San Francisco buildings already renting server space, plus a 10 megawatt proposal at the Cow Palace marketed as emergency response infrastructure rather than a data center.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The moratorium at the center of the congressional race applies above 20 megawatts, and everything already operating in San Francisco sits below it. Servers were for rent at 274 Brannan Street and 200 Paul Avenue with diesel backup generators on the air district's books. The argument between Connie Chan and Scott Wiener ran on labels, and the labels did not reach the buildings people walk past.

top_stories.source_headline: Handshake, not a drug deal? San Francisco police drone case falls apart.
top_stories.one_line: A San Francisco drug case collapsed after defense counsel argued the police drone footage showed a handshake rather than a sale, and the defendant had already spent four days in jail.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: SFPD says the Real Time Investigations Center helped make more than 500 arrests last year, and this dismissal is the only one of them the public has been able to inspect. The center is a police unit built with private money from Chris Larsen, Steve Huffman, Michael Seibel and the Moritz family foundation, and Proposition E removed the requirement that the police commission or the supervisors approve its tools. Larsen also gave $10 million last week to fight the state's billionaire tax.

pattern_of_the_week.title: The rule was never where the decision was
pattern_of_the_week.note:
Twelve of the week's eighteen items describe a rule that exists somewhere other than where the outcome gets decided. State inspectors visited a SoMa childcare center 13 times in four years and substantiated violations, and the center closed in May because the money ran out. San Francisco's 2019 facial recognition ban binds city government only, so Flock, whose 483 license plate readers cover the city from the Tenderloin to Seacliff, took out a California private investigator license instead. The sheriff's body camera policy stops recording when a television production starts the interview. The data center moratorium both congressional candidates are arguing about sets its floor at 20 megawatts, above every server hall already running on Brannan Street and Paul Avenue. The tenant protections called the strongest in the nation do not reach the subtenant layer. The rent algorithm ban has produced zero lawsuits in two years.

These are not enforcement failures. They are rules written against a mechanism that had already moved, and the outcome now turns on who holds the money, the license, the LLC, or the contract. Two items showed the same thing from the other direction: a police surveillance unit built with private donations after Proposition E removed the approval requirement, and a county Democratic Party that rewrote its endorsement rule one week after the billionaire tax qualified for the ballot. Both moved a decision out of the room where it used to be made. When the rule is in the wrong place, changing the rule is the cheapest thing a city can do and the least likely to matter.
connections: Licensing that documented 13 visits to a SoMa childcare center and never closed it, while the money did.
A data center moratorium set at 20 megawatts in a city whose existing server halls and its newest 10 megawatt proposal both sit under the line.
A camera vendor with 483 readers in San Francisco taking out a private investigator license, and a body camera policy that stops recording when a TV crew starts the interview.
Tenant protections with no reach into the subtenant layer, and an algorithm ban with zero lawsuits while asking rents rose 14 percent between March and July.
A police unit built with private donations after Proposition E dropped the approval requirement, and a county party that changed its endorsement rule a week after Prop. 40 qualified.
